summary:
Bremen stands under the federal framework. The Self-Determination Act (SBGG) took effect on 1 November 2024, having passed the Bundestag by 374 votes to 251. Adults over 18 may change their legal gender by self-declaration without the former medical or court pathway, and the change is entered in the civil registry. Bremen has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement series of its own; the city-state's registry offices process declarations under the unchanged federal act, and federal criminal law and the general equality act apply without local deviation.

The sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor is custody. German prison administration is a state competence, and Bremen has no placement statute of its own, so the national framework governs inmate placement. All Länder tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender, and § 6(1) SBGG permits state law to override the registry entry; many Länder have enacted exception clauses, some abstract in wording and others criticised as targeting trans inmates specifically. Placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been applied only exceptionally in practice.

The Liebich case shows how the exception works in practice. Marla-Svenja Liebich's gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act; after her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was placed in a men's prison despite her legal registration as a woman, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. A 16 July 2026 France24 wire report on the case records that Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia responded by launching a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal act.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Germany since 1 October 2017 and has no Bremen-specific restriction, so a partner's status travels on the ordinary federal footing.
tangentialFactors:
The prison-placement debate is a federal-level exposure for every Land, not a local Bremen matter. The Verfassungsblog framework analysis of 18 March 2026 records that Länder with their own exception clauses are acting under the permission § 6(1) SBGG grants them, and that some of those clauses have been criticised as trans-targeted while others are framed as applying abstractly to all inmates.

State-level variation around the federal act is active. Rhineland-Palatinate took a new § 17 of its prison act into force on 1 March 2026 to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and the Berlin prison service maintains a public information page in German for trans, inter and non-binary persons held in its facilities. Bremen has no equivalent local instrument on file; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony is running a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison and reads the Lower Saxony correctional act as requiring binary men and women housing with gender-identity placement only in exceptional cases.

State and federal responses to the Liebich case diverge in emphasis. Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia moved to restrict the federal act rather than to expand placement flexibility, a direction a visitor in Bremen should expect to see echoed in Länder-level political debate even though Bremen itself has not legislated.
localsOnly:
Bremen registry offices carry out SBGG declarations directly; a resident of the city-state changes their legal gender through the same federal self-declaration route used in every other Land, with no local medical or court gate and no local waiting period.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Germany since 1 October 2017 and is available on the standard federal footing in Bremen, including for partner and family recognition.

Bremen has no local statute, ordinance, guidance series or designated office on trans matters beyond operating the federal act. A resident seeking prison placement corresponding to gender identity must argue within the federal framework and the Länder prison acts, since Bremen has enacted no placement rule of its own.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: how the gender-identity placement exception is applied in Bremen's own correctional facilities is not sourced. The Verfassungsblog analysis confirms Bremen has no placement statute, but no Bremen-specific intake or review practice is on file.

Unresolved: whether the Bundesrat initiative launched by Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia after the Liebich case has advanced beyond proposal stage, and what effect any tightened federal act would have on Bremen, is not documented in the sources held.

Not sourced for Bremen: any local hostile-offence series, hate-crime reporting pattern or event-security finding. Practical hostility risk tracks the national position, and the national support machinery, including the STOP the HATE counselling finder, crisis line and hate-crime knowledge base, is available to residents and visitors alike.

Not sourced for Bremen: how the city-state's facilities handle access to women-protected spaces such as saunas, pools and shelters after the national act took effect on 1 January 2025. The guideline debate recorded for the sector at large has no Bremen-specific outcome on file.

The federal criminal-law history recorded for the country, including Nazi-era tightening of Section 175a, is retained only as background to the regime Bremen sits under and carries no current trans-specific enforcement finding.
